name: Rafael Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and became the junior manager of four dispatch clerks at a large company's depot this spring. I have a bachelor's degree, but most of what I know came from years at the departures desk; I still lean on senior clerk Marta when a plan gets complicated. I like solving a late load with one phone call and hate sitting over a report I know someone else could check faster.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the day look like when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works part time in the school kitchen, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. My manager pay is at the low end and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few similar posts nearby, so I don't talk about leaving lightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I'd say a faster form is fine, but the dispatch clerks still need to ring a driver when a load is late. I wouldn't tell my team our day changes much under AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I only became their manager this spring, after years on the desk, and I still ask my senior clerk to check my weekly plan. My partner works part time at the school kitchen, our two children are in school, and the mortgage leaves us with less than a month saved; even a steady job feels tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll run the departure board the usual way and double-check any automatic time estimate against the driver's call. In the first year of this plateau, we'll stop buying takeaway on Fridays, about 40 a month, and put that amount into a small mortgage buffer if nothing else breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills, though I am not frightened of this small AI change. A missed school shift or a car repair could put us behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would press you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill comes just after the mortgage, and we don't have room for both to rise. My brother could help once, but I don't want to make a habit of asking him to cover our basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your senior clerk check for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta checks whether I have put two deliveries on one driver's legal rest period. I am still learning the manager side. Admitting I still need my senior clerk's help is safer than pretending a form made me expert.

say: I'd say **driver calls** still matter when a load is late, even if forms get faster.
I'd tell my clerks their **daily work** stays mostly familiar in this picture.
think: I am a **new manager** who still needs a senior clerk's check on weekly plans.
The **mortgage and bills** leave less than one month saved despite stable work.
do: Run the **departure board** and check automatic times against driver calls.
Stop **Friday takeaways** and put roughly 40 monthly into a mortgage buffer if bills allow.
feel: He feels **anxious** about existing bills, though small AI changes do not frighten him.
S0.quote: Admitting I still need my senior clerk's help is safer than pretending a form made me expert.
fieldNote: His **thin buffer** and partner's part-time shifts explain anxiety even when the job barely changes.
He names a **real planning gap** and relies on Marta's rest-period check rather than a software claim.

steps.text: Run the departure board and verify estimated times by driver calls
Stop Friday takeaways to free about 40 monthly
Put the freed 40 monthly into mortgage cash if bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the dispatch team Steady Disruption means booking and planning systems will do more of our screen work, and the company needs to explain who stays. I'd ask for proper training before any clerk is judged on a new dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I am the newest manager and the weakest at the planning reports, so I could be the first post folded into another depot. My partner's school hours won't cover the mortgage if my pay stops, and there are few manager jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the depot manager for the staffing timetable and keep a written record of the calls that changed a delivery. In the first year of disruption, if our rota is cut, I'd ask the local haulage firm about a dispatch supervisor opening before giving notice, and drop the children's paid weekend sports only if we cannot cover the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I imagine carrying the redundancy letter home. I am slow with new tools. The bills will not wait for me to become quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about sport?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them we might need to use the free school field for a while, not that their matches don't matter. I'd talk to my partner first, because the fee is 70 a month and the cut only happens if our income falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course on the dashboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company paid for time with a trainer beside me, I would attend and practise on old dispatch records. I won't promise to master it from a link sent at midnight.

say: I'd ask for a **staffing timetable** as booking and planning move to software.
I'd seek **paid training** before clerks are judged by a new dashboard.
think: My **new manager post** could be folded into another depot before I master the reports.
School-kitchen pay cannot cover our **mortgage**, and nearby manager openings are scarce.
do: Request the **staffing timetable** and record delivery-changing calls this week.
Learn the **AI dashboard** on old records with a trainer if company time is paid.
Ask about a **dispatch vacancy** if cut; pause sports fees only if household income falls.
feel: He feels **alarmed** about carrying a redundancy letter home with a mortgage due.
S1.quote: The bills will not wait for me to become quick.
fieldNote: He expects a **manager-level cut** because his promotion is recent and his reports are still weak.
The sports fee is a **conditional last cut**, and dashboard learning requires paid time with a trainer.

steps.text: Learn AI dashboard with a trainer on old records if company pays for time
Ask the local haulage firm about a dispatch supervisor vacancy if cut
Pause paid weekend sports only if household income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 means the depot can buy planning skill more cheaply than it can pay us, and staff need notice before positions vanish. I'd ask the company to name who takes responsibility for a wrong delivery order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and calls on my desk could change in 2028, while robots doing the loading arrive around 2031; that later date doesn't save my manager job. With less than a month in cash, I think a lost paycheck would put the mortgage at risk almost at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask my brother whether he could take us in for two weeks if the mortgage payment became impossible, and I will gather my dispatch certificates and driver references. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post goes, I'd apply for a driving role at the depot only if an actual vacancy exists and the pay covers the mortgage; I'd check job-loss support eligibility before claiming anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and ashamed that I have so little saved at 43. I can make calls, but I cannot make the next mortgage payment with a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner this evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the account balance and the mortgage date, then ask which expenses we could stop before the children notice. We already cancelled the holiday, so there is no big spare luxury waiting to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take driving work after managing clerks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I pass the required driving check and the wage pays our mortgage. I have an older licence, but I would need to confirm what the depot requires now; I won't tell the family I have a job before an offer is signed.

say: I'd demand **notice** and a named person accountable for wrong AGI dispatch orders.
I'd tell staff **planning work** changes in 2028, before loading robots arrive.
think: My **desk job** faces 2028 AGI; 2031 loading robots give me no extra shelter.
Less than one month saved makes a missed wage an immediate **mortgage threat**.
do: Ask my **brother** now about two weeks of shelter and gather driving references.
After 2028, seek **driving work** only if there is a vacancy, required check passes and pay covers mortgage.
feel: He feels **alarmed** by the mortgage risk and ashamed of the thin reserve.
S2.quote: I cannot make the next mortgage payment with a promise.
fieldNote: The fast case threatens **2028 thinking tasks**, while robot loading in 2031 changes a different part of the depot.
His driving fallback has **three conditions**: a vacancy, qualification check and enough pay for the mortgage.

steps.text: Ask brother about two weeks of shelter if mortgage payment fails
Apply for depot driving only if vacancy, licence check and mortgage-covering pay align

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn what part of dispatch still needs people and to ask for proper apprenticeships. I want the company to stop calling a one-hour video a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could take our eldest through secondary school and give me time to rebuild a cash buffer. The planning system still reaches my desk in 2031, before robots around 2034 take hands-on loading; I cannot count on the later date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning next spring, if the local transport college has an affordable place, I'd take its evening vehicle-maintenance course and learn to diagnose basic faults myself. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for workshop coordinator jobs only where the wage pays the mortgage and the employer has an opening; until then I'd keep my depot post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than trapped. Five years gives me a chance to learn slowly, but our cash will not grow by wishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college fee is 300 for the term, and I'd enrol only if we can put that amount aside without missing the mortgage. My partner and I would make the decision together before I pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance after years in dispatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know which faults delay a truck, but I do not know how to fix them. I would rather learn with a mechanic nearby than claim my office experience makes me one.

say: I'd ask for **proper apprenticeships** before dispatch planning changes in 2031.
I'd reject a **one-hour video** presented as training for a new trade.
think: Five years might let the family build **cash** and finish a school stage.
AGI reaches my **desk in 2031**; 2034 loading robots do not delay that.
do: Take an **evening maintenance course** next spring if the place and 300 fee are affordable.
Seek **workshop coordinator work** after 2031 only with a vacancy and mortgage-covering pay.
feel: He feels **anxious** but sees five years to learn at a manageable pace.
S3.quote: I would rather learn with a mechanic nearby than claim my office experience makes me one.
fieldNote: His choice of **maintenance** builds from faults he knows but admits he cannot yet repair.
The **300 fee** and mortgage payment determine whether the course is possible, not enthusiasm alone.

steps.text: Take evening vehicle-maintenance course if a place opens and 300 is affordable
Apply for workshop coordinator openings after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives working parents time to prepare if employers give real training dates. I would ask for a course list now rather than a promise to talk about it in nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AI arrives, and I could have children finishing school and a smaller mortgage by then. I still do not like new software, but a decade might let me build a practical trade without throwing away today's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep managing the departure desk and ask the college when its next maintenance course runs, then take it only if the fee fits after mortgage and school costs. In the first year after 2036, I'd stay if the depot has a paid workshop role for me, or apply to the nearby repair firms if they have vacancies; I wouldn't resign to chase a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about starting again in my fifties, but there is enough time to make small, paid-for moves. I still worry about the next electricity bill today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older child likes engines and sometimes helps our neighbour clean tools, but I won't put our mortgage on a child's future income. I can ask my brother for advice on workshops without making him pay the course fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good course give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want supervised hours on real vehicles and a record an employer recognizes. I need to show a mechanic's work, not carry another paper that says I watched a video.

say: I'd ask for **training dates** and course lists now, even with AGI a decade away.
I'd tell working parents to keep **current wages** while preparing.
think: At **53**, I may have a smaller mortgage and children finishing school.
I still avoid new software, but a **practical trade** could be learned over time.
do: Keep **managing departures** this year and ask the college for its next course date.
Take **maintenance training** only if mortgage and school costs allow.
After 2036, stay for a **paid workshop role** or apply to nearby repair firms with vacancies.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about retraining in his fifties and still worries about bills now.
S4.quote: I need to show a mechanic's work, not carry another paper that says I watched a video.
fieldNote: The decade allows **gradual training** while he keeps wages, but current bills still drive anxiety.
He rejects making **children's income** or his brother's money the basis of a family plan.

steps.text: Keep running the depot departure desk this year
Take vehicle-maintenance training if mortgage and school costs permit
Apply for paid workshop vacancies after 2036 without resigning first

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lost dispatch wage could put the mortgage behind almost immediately. Real notice, a funded practical course, and an actual local vacancy with pay we can live on would help more than a promise that everyone will find something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the driver when a perfect-looking schedule breaks the rest rules. A dispatch clerk must check a driver's rest hours before releasing the schedule.

headlineQuote: A dispatch clerk must check a driver's rest hours before releasing the schedule.
portrait: At **43**, Rafael is a newly promoted junior dispatch manager who still asks a senior clerk to check plans.
His **thin reserve**, low pay, part-time household income and mortgage make even AI Plateau financially anxious.
He avoids **AI tools**, looks for paid practical instruction and refuses to resign without a real offer.
Fast AGI threatens the **mortgage**; longer runways allow a conditional move toward vehicle-maintenance work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his desk wage before he has enough cash to protect the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Real notice**, funded practical training and a local vacancy with mortgage-covering pay would make a move possible.
